text:
We spent the last five months rebuilding our search. I want to write down what actually happened rather than the version that will end up in the case study.

The old search was a LIKE query against a products table with 400,000 rows and no full text index, which worked fine in 2019 when there were 12,000 rows. By the time anyone looked at it properly, the p95 was 2.8 seconds and about 30% of searches returned nothing at all, mostly because of plurals and spelling.

We moved to Elasticsearch. The migration itself took three weeks. The other four months went to relevance tuning, which nobody warned me about and which turned out to be the entire job. Getting results back fast is an engineering problem. Getting the right results back is an argument between three departments about what right means.

Where we landed: p95 is 140ms, zero-result searches are down to 6%, and conversion from search is up about 11% year on year, though I would not swear that is all us because we also changed the product images in the same quarter.

The part I would redo: we should have shipped the plural and spelling handling on the old system in week one. It was two days of work and it would have bought us four months of goodwill.

text:
Long post about our hiring process, because someone asked and the answer does not fit in a comment.

We get roughly 300 applications for a backend role. Two people screen them, which takes about six hours each. We move maybe 25 to a first call.

The first call is 30 minutes and I do most of them myself. I ask what they worked on most recently and then I ask follow-up questions until either I understand the system or it becomes clear they do not. That is the whole screen. No puzzles, no trivia.

About 10 go to the technical session. That is two hours, paired, on a branch of our actual repository with a real ticket from our backlog. We pay for it if it runs long. Roughly half the people who do it get an offer.

The part I am least happy about: our time from application to offer is 24 days on average and we have lost at least four people to faster companies. I do not have a fix that does not involve cutting something I think is load bearing.

The part that works better than I expected: candidates tell us the paired session was the most enjoyable interview they have had in years. Two people who did not get offers have since referred friends to us.

text:
Postmortem for our outage on the 9th, shared publicly because we told customers we would.

At 14:02 IST a routine deploy of the notifications service went out. At 14:04 the service began returning 500s on about 40% of requests. Full recovery at 15:11. Sixty-nine minutes.

Cause: the deploy included a dependency bump that changed the default TLS verification behaviour of our HTTP client. Our internal certificate authority is not in the default trust store, so calls to two internal services started failing. This did not surface in staging because staging talks to those services over plaintext inside the cluster.

Why it took an hour: the error we logged was a generic connection failure, and the first thirty minutes went to investigating a network change that had happened the same morning and was entirely unrelated. Classic.

Actions, with owners and dates, not vibes:
1. Staging uses the same TLS path as production. Priya, by the 30th.
2. The HTTP client wrapper logs the underlying TLS error rather than swallowing it. Karthik, this week.
3. Dependency bumps for anything touching transport get a separate deploy, not a bundled one. Already in the runbook.

We did not lose data. Notifications queued during the window were delivered by 15:40, out of order in some cases, which we know is annoying for anyone who received them.

text:
I have been reviewing our accessibility backlog and I want to say something about how it got this long.

We have 61 open accessibility issues. 40 of them were filed by the same two people. Nothing in our process stops an inaccessible component from shipping, and nothing prioritises fixing one afterwards, so the backlog is where these go to be counted rather than fixed.

The things actually broken, roughly in order of how much they matter: our modal traps focus incorrectly so a keyboard user can tab behind it into the page; our form errors are announced as generic text rather than being associated with the field; three of our five chart types have no text alternative at all; and our primary button colour fails contrast against the background we most often put it on, which we have known since a design review in 2023.

We are fixing the modal and the form errors this quarter because they are the ones that make the product unusable rather than unpleasant. The charts need a real design conversation and I am not going to pretend it will happen before June.

I am writing this partly as a commitment device. If it is still 61 issues in September, someone should send me this post.

text:
Thoughts after a year of using our own product every day, which we did not do for the first two years and should have.

Things I found that no customer ever reported: the session expires at 30 minutes, and if you are mid-form when it happens, you lose the form. Every single one of us had learned to copy our text before submitting. Nobody had filed a ticket about it because we had all adapted.

That is the thing about dogfooding that surprised me. It does not surface the bugs people complain about. It surfaces the ones people have quietly built habits around, which are usually worse.

We fixed the session thing in a day. It had been there for four years.

The other change: I now know how slow our reports page is on a bad connection, because I used it from a train. Two minutes. Our internal testing all happens on office fibre, so it has always looked fine.

Not a revelation, I know. But there is a difference between knowing you should use your own product and having the calendar reality of actually doing it, and we only got there by making one person's job include it.

text:
We ran a proper retrospective on a project that failed and I want to record what came out of it, because most failure writeups I read are secretly about how the failure was noble.

The project was a customer portal. Eight months, four engineers, one designer. It shipped and roughly 4% of the customers it was built for have used it more than once.

What we got wrong, in the order it happened:

We validated the idea with the people who asked for it, who were the account managers, not the customers. The account managers wanted customers to self-serve so they would stop answering the same email. That is a real problem, but it is their problem, not the customer's problem.

We never talked to a customer until month six. When we did, the first one said she would rather email her account manager because then she has a record and a person to chase.

We kept going after that conversation, because we were two months from shipping and stopping felt more expensive than finishing. That was the actual mistake. The eight months were sunk by then, the last two were a choice.

What we are changing: nothing ships without three conversations with the people who will use it, held in the first month, recorded, with the questions written before the call so we do not lead them. We have said versions of this before. This time it is in the project template as a gate, which is the only mechanism that has ever worked here.

text:
A practical writeup on moving our team from Jira to plain GitHub issues, four months in, including the parts that are worse.

Better: the work is where the code is, so nobody context switches to update status. Our issue hygiene went from about half the tickets being stale to almost none, purely because closing an issue is now a side effect of merging.

Better: engineers actually read the backlog now. In eighteen months of Jira I never once saw someone browse the backlog voluntarily.

Worse: reporting. Our head of delivery used to pull a burndown in two clicks and now I write a script. She is being gracious about it, and the honest position is that we moved a cost from nine engineers to one manager, which is a good trade for the nine and a bad one for her.

Worse: cross-team dependencies. We have three repositories and an issue that spans two of them lives in neither properly. Jira handled this and GitHub does not, and the workaround is a checklist in a third issue, which is exactly as bad as it sounds.

Would I do it again: yes, at nine people. At forty, no. I think that is the whole answer and I do not think it generalises past our size.

text:
On the question of whether to rewrite or refactor, from someone who has now done both badly.

In 2021 we rewrote a payments integration from scratch. It took five months against an estimate of six weeks. The rewrite was correct on the happy path in about three weeks. The other four months were the seventeen edge cases the old code handled that nobody had documented, each discovered in production, several of them involving refunds, one of them involving a regulator.

In 2023 we refactored a scheduling module instead. Twelve weeks, incremental, tests added before each change, feature flag per behaviour. It was tedious and it worked and nobody outside the team noticed, which is the correct outcome.

What I take from those two: the old code's ugliness is usually the record of the requirements. If you cannot enumerate why each ugly branch exists, you do not understand the system well enough to replace it, and the rewrite is a bet that the branches were not important.

Sometimes they are not important. The 2021 code also had 400 lines of dead retry logic for a payment provider we left in 2018. But we found that out by reading it, not by deleting it and waiting.

text:
Notes on running a clinic front desk, written for the software people who keep trying to sell me products.

We see between 60 and 80 patients a day across four doctors. The front desk is two people, one of whom is also handling insurance paperwork.

The actual bottleneck is not scheduling and it is not billing. It is that a patient arrives, and we need to know within about fifteen seconds whether they are here for a first consultation, a follow-up within the free window, a procedure that needs pre-authorisation, or a report collection. Four different flows, decided at the counter, while the person is standing there and three others are queued behind them.

Every system I have been shown solves the calendar. The calendar was never hard. What I want is a screen that shows me who is in the waiting room right now, colour coded by what they need, updated when the doctor finishes with someone.

We currently do this with a whiteboard. The whiteboard has been more reliable than the two systems we bought and abandoned, and I say that as someone who would genuinely like to stop using a whiteboard.

text:
I want to talk about what a year of trying to hire a senior data engineer taught me about our own job description.

We opened the role in January. We closed it in November with an internal transfer. In between we spoke to 31 people.

The description asked for Spark, Airflow, dbt, Kafka, Snowflake, Terraform, and "strong SQL". Every candidate who had all of those was either at a company paying 40% more than us or wanted to work on something bigger than our 200GB of data.

The person we eventually moved into the role knew SQL extremely well, had never touched Kafka, and had spent three years as an analyst arguing with our data, which meant she already knew where every bad join in the warehouse was.

Six months in she has removed more problems than the job description would have predicted, and she learned Airflow in a fortnight because Airflow is not the hard part.

I am not making the argument that skills do not matter. I am making the narrower argument that we wrote down the tools we use instead of the problems we have, and then we spent eleven months looking for someone who matched a list.

text:
Our engineering onboarding document was 40 pages and nobody read it. Here is what we replaced it with and what happened.

We deleted 31 pages. What survived: how to get access to things, how to run the app locally, how deploys work, who to ask about what, and a single annotated walkthrough of one request from the load balancer to the database and back.

That last one is the only part anyone has thanked me for. It is four pages and it took two days to write because I had to check things I thought I knew.

The 31 deleted pages were mostly history. Why we chose Postgres. Why the billing service is separate. The 2022 architecture decision records. All of that is real and useful and none of it is useful in week one.

We moved it to a folder called background and told people to read it in month two. As far as I can tell nobody has, which is either fine or is telling me something I do not want to hear about how much of our written history matters.

Time for a new engineer to open their first pull request went from about nine days to three. Most of that is the access section, which is now a script.

text:
Reflections on eleven years of teaching mathematics to fourteen year olds, prompted by a colleague asking if I am tired of it.

I am not tired of the teaching. I am tired of the reporting. This year I will write roughly 340 individual comments, each of which must reference a specific piece of evidence and a next step, for a system that produces a document most parents skim in ninety seconds.

The teaching itself has got better. Specifically: I stopped explaining a method and then giving twenty practice questions. I now give three questions, two of which the method handles cleanly and one of which it does not, and we spend the lesson on the one that does not.

My top set hated this for about six weeks because it felt slower and they are optimised for speed. The middle set took to it immediately. The bottom set, where I expected disaster, has been the biggest surprise, because the third question does not have a right answer they are failing to reach.

The exam results are essentially unchanged. I am aware this undermines my case somewhat. But the questions the students ask me now are better questions, and I do not have a metric for that, and I am choosing to believe it anyway.

text:
We migrated 14 years of files off a Windows file server and I have opinions about digital hoarding now.

2.1 terabytes. 940,000 files. The oldest ones were from 2010 and were Word documents saved by people who left before I joined.

What we found when we actually looked: about 60% of the volume was duplicated. Not similar, byte identical. The same board pack existing in eleven folders because eleven people had saved it. Another 15% was one department's scanned PDFs of documents that also exist in the accounting system.

We kept everything, because deciding what to delete would have cost more than the storage does, and because deleting the wrong thing in a regulated business is not a mistake you make twice. But we deduplicated and the actual unique content is about 500GB.

The part that surprised me: nobody has requested a file older than 2019 in the eight months since the migration. Not once. We have all this and we use the last four years of it.

I do not have a tidy conclusion. We are paying to store the professional memory of a company that does not consult its memory.

text:
A note on estimates, from someone who has been wrong about them for a long time and has stopped trying to be right.

We tracked every estimate against actuals for two quarters. 38 pieces of work. The median piece took 1.7 times its estimate. The mean took 2.4, which tells you there were some real disasters in there.

But here is the useful bit. When we split by whether the work touched a system the estimator had personally worked on before, the median for familiar systems was 1.1. For unfamiliar ones it was 2.9.

So our estimates are not bad. Our estimates of unfamiliar work are bad, and we were averaging the two together and concluding that estimation is impossible.

What we do now: an estimate comes with a note about familiarity, and anything marked unfamiliar gets a two day spike before it gets a number. The spike is not free, it is roughly 8% of our capacity, and it has taken our overall multiplier from 1.7 to about 1.3.

That is not a transformation and I am not going to sell it as one. It is a fifth of our overrun, recovered, for a cost we can see.

I run the logistics for a mid-sized distributor and I want to describe what a normal Tuesday actually involves, because I read a lot of supply chain content that does not resemble my job.

We move about 400 orders a day out of one warehouse to roughly 90 retailers. Four trucks, two of them ours, two contracted.

Today: one truck did not arrive because the contractor double-booked. That is 90 orders that need to go on other vehicles or wait. Deciding which ones wait is the job, and it is not an optimisation problem, it is a relationship problem, because two of those retailers will call my director and two will not, and the ones who will not call are the ones we have been letting down for six weeks.

Our system tells me delivery windows and stock levels. It does not tell me who is out of patience. That lives in my head and in a notebook, and when I was on leave in October the person covering had no way to know it and made entirely defensible decisions that cost us an account.

Every vendor who has demoed to me wants to show me route optimisation. Our routes are basically fixed. I want to encode the notebook.

Three months after switching our team to trunk based development, an honest account.

Before: feature branches, average lifetime eleven days, merge conflicts constantly, and a release process that took a full afternoon and required one specific person.

Now: everything goes to main behind a flag, we deploy about nine times a day, and releases are not an event.

The good is obvious and I will not belabour it. The costs, which nobody mentioned to me:

Our flag count went from zero to 34 in two months, and roughly a third of them are dead. Nobody removes a flag once the feature is out, because removing it is work with no visible benefit. We now have a fortnightly flag cleanup that everyone hates and that I will defend forever.

Code review changed character. Reviews are smaller, which is better, but the design conversation that used to happen on a big pull request now happens nowhere unless someone deliberately schedules it. We lost something there and I have not fully replaced it.

And one engineer is genuinely unhappy. He liked long branches and deep focus and he experiences the new rhythm as constant interruption. I do not think he is wrong. I think we optimised for the team at a real cost to him and I have not found a way to give it back.

text:
Someone asked me to write up how we do incident response at a company with nine engineers and no dedicated ops team, so here it is, unglamorous.

One person is on call for a week. They carry a phone. If it rings outside hours, they get the next morning off, and that is honoured without negotiation because the first time we negotiated it we lost the goodwill for a year.

We have four alerts that page. Four. Everything else goes to a channel that nobody is obliged to read at night. Getting from about sixty alerts to four took a quarter and mostly consisted of asking, for each alert, whether we would genuinely wake a person for it. For fifty-six of them the answer was no.

When something happens the on-call person's first job is to say in the channel that they are on it. Not to fix it. To say it. This sounds trivial and it eliminated the thing where three people independently debug the same problem and one of them restarts something under the others.

We write a postmortem for anything customer-visible over five minutes. It is a page. It has a timeline, a cause, and actions with names and dates. No blameless-culture language, because we are nine people and everybody already knows who deployed it, and pretending otherwise is more corrosive than just being decent about it.

What I learned auditing our own analytics after discovering our signup number was wrong for eight months.

The dashboard said 1,200 signups a month. The database said about 900. Nobody noticed because the dashboard number was the one in the board pack and the database number was the one nobody queried.

Cause: the tracking event fired on the form submit, not on successful account creation. So every failed signup, every duplicate email, every validation error counted as a signup. Roughly 25% of form submits fail, which is its own problem and one I would not have found otherwise.

The embarrassing part is that we made decisions on the wrong number. We concluded our Q2 campaign worked. Recalculated, it was flat. We spent about 6 lakh extending it.

What we changed: every metric on the executive dashboard now has a link to the query or the event definition behind it, and one person is responsible for reconciling the top five against the database monthly. It takes her about two hours.

What I actually think the lesson is: not that we should verify our metrics, which everyone already agrees with in the abstract, but that a number becomes true by being repeated in meetings, and there was no moment where anyone was supposed to check.

A year of trying to reduce our carbon reporting burden, described honestly for other people in operations roles who have been handed this.

We are a 180 person manufacturing business. In 2024 our largest customer began requiring scope 1, 2 and partial scope 3 data as a condition of the contract. Nobody here had done this before and I got it because I had a spreadsheet reputation.

Scope 1 and 2 were tedious but tractable. Fuel receipts, electricity bills, twelve months of data, about three weeks of work including finding out that two of our meters had been billed on estimates since 2022.

Scope 3 is where it falls apart. It requires data from suppliers, and 40 of our 60 suppliers either do not have it or will not share it. The accepted practice is to use industry average emission factors, which means a substantial part of the number I am submitting is an average multiplied by our spend. It is defensible. It is also not a measurement of anything we did.

I am not writing this to be cynical about the reporting. The scope 1 work found real waste, and we cut gas usage 14% by fixing a compressor schedule. I am writing it because the confident single number at the end of these reports conceals an enormous difference in how much of it is measured and how much is arithmetic on a spend column.

text:
We killed our chatbot after fourteen months and I want to write down why, in case it is useful to someone about to build one.

It handled 31% of incoming conversations without a human. That number was in every deck and it is real. What the number does not say is which 31%.

When we looked, the automated conversations were almost entirely password resets, order status, and opening hours. All three of those already had a self-serve page. What the bot was actually doing was giving people who could not find the page a slower way to reach the same information, and we counted that as deflection.

Meanwhile the conversations that mattered, where somebody was upset about a delivery or confused about a charge, were being routed through two or three bot turns before reaching a person, and our satisfaction scores for those conversations were nine points lower than for conversations that started with a human.

We replaced it with a better search on the help pages and a form that routes directly. Handle time went up, because now humans handle the hard ones and the easy ones do not become conversations at all. Total conversations dropped by a fifth.

I do not think chatbots are useless. I think we measured the thing that was easy to measure and then defended it for a year.

Some thoughts on remote work from a company that has been fully distributed since 2019, so before it was fashionable and after it stopped being.

What has consistently worked: written decisions. Anything agreed in a call gets written in a channel within the day, by the person who called the meeting. We have done this for five years and it is the single practice I would keep if I could keep one.

What has consistently not worked: our attempts at social connection. We have tried virtual coffee, games, a book club, and a channel for pets. All of them run for six weeks on the enthusiasm of one organiser and then stop. I have concluded that we cannot manufacture this and I have stopped trying, which some people read as giving up and which I read as being honest about what a company can provide.

What surprised me: onboarding is harder remotely and stays harder for about four months, not four weeks. New people are missing the incidental context that in-person work delivers for free, and the only thing that has helped is deliberately over-inviting them to conversations they do not obviously need to be in.

What I would tell a company going distributed now: your bottleneck will not be tools. It will be that every implicit thing has to become explicit, and half your senior people communicate implicitly and do not know it.

Two years into using infrastructure as code properly, here is the state of things including the parts that annoy me.

Everything in AWS is in Terraform except for two things: the certificate for our apex domain, which was created by hand in 2019 by someone who left and which I am afraid to touch, and an SQS queue that a lambda creates at runtime, which is a design mistake we have not paid to fix.

Good: rebuilding our staging environment from nothing takes 40 minutes and one command. We do it monthly, deliberately, so that we know it still works. The first time we tried it took four days because of exactly the kind of hand-created drift I described above.

Annoying: the plan output for any change to our networking module is 300 lines and nobody reads it properly. We have approved changes we did not understand. Twice this caused an outage, both times brief.

Also annoying: our modules have become their own codebase, with versioning and a changelog and a deprecation policy, and I now employ roughly a third of a person maintaining the thing that was supposed to reduce work.

Still worth it. But the honest accounting is that we traded a class of problem we understood for a class of problem we are still learning, and the second class has better tooling and worse intuition.

Writing this up because three people have asked me the same question this month about pricing changes.

We raised prices 22% in April on new customers only. Existing customers were grandfathered indefinitely, which we announced clearly.

What happened to conversion: our trial to paid rate went from 14.2% to 13.6% over the following four months. That is a real drop and it is smaller than the price increase, so revenue per trial went up meaningfully.

What happened that I did not predict: about 30 existing customers wrote in to ask if they should upgrade or lock in, and eleven of them upgraded to annual plans to feel secure about it. So the announcement itself generated revenue from people whose prices had not changed.

What I got wrong: I spent two weeks writing a careful email explaining the reasoning, the cost increases, the additional features. Our head of support suggested a three sentence version. We sent hers. Nobody asked for the reasoning.

The grandfathering is now a liability we carry forever, and in five years someone will suggest ending it and there will be a bad week. I made that trade knowingly and I would make it again, but it is a trade and not a free choice.

Notes from six months of being the only technical person at a nonprofit, after fifteen years at software companies.

The technology is not the problem. The problem is that there are eleven systems, nine of which were set up by a volunteer or a consultant who is gone, and each of which holds a slightly different version of the same list of people.

Our donor list exists in the CRM, the email tool, a Google Sheet maintained by the fundraising lead, and the accounting system. None of them agree. When someone dies, we find out because a family member calls us upset that we sent a letter, and then I update it in four places and probably miss one.

What I have done so far: made the CRM authoritative, written a weekly sync from CRM to email tool, and deleted the sheet after copying its unique data across. The accounting system stays separate because integrating it is a two month project and the finance officer, reasonably, does not want her ledger written to by a script I wrote.

What I have learned: at a software company, technical debt costs you velocity. Here it costs you dignity in your relationship with a grieving family. Same category of problem, entirely different weight, and it has changed how I prioritise.

text:
I have spent the last month reading our own API documentation as if I were a new customer and I want to record what that was like.

The reference is complete. Every endpoint, every field, generated from the schema, always current. This is the part we are proud of and it is genuinely good.

The problem is that it is the only thing we have. There is no page that says what the objects mean or how they relate. A new developer arrives, finds 60 endpoints, and has no way to learn that an Account contains Subscriptions, a Subscription has exactly one Plan, and that our Invoice object predates all of this and attaches to the Account rather than the Subscription for historical reasons that affect how you should query it.

I know this because I have explained it verbally to about twenty customers.

So I wrote one page. A diagram, five paragraphs, and three worked examples of common tasks. It took a week, most of which was arguing with myself about the invoice thing.

Support questions tagged as integration have dropped by roughly a third since it went up. I am not going to claim causation from one month of data, but I will say that the generated reference, which took a quarter to build, has never moved that number.

An account of our attempt to reduce meeting load, including the part where it partially failed.

We started at an average of 14 hours a week in meetings per engineer, measured from calendars over a month.

We cancelled every recurring meeting for two weeks and let people re-add what they missed. This is the advice everyone gives. Here is what actually happened.

Seven meetings came back immediately, which was fine and informative. Three did not come back, and two months later it became clear that two of them had been doing something. Specifically, the cross-team sync that nobody re-added had been the only place where the mobile team heard about API changes, and we shipped a breaking change in September that cost them a week.

So the meeting had a function that was invisible to the people in it, including me, and it only became visible after it was gone.

We are now at about 9 hours a week, which I am happy with. The cross-team sync is back, at half the length, with a written agenda.

The lesson I take is not that the reset was wrong. It is that the two week window was too short to observe the consequences, and I presented the result as a success in week three when I did not yet know.

text:
Some numbers on our apprenticeship programme, three cohorts in, because I keep being asked whether it is worth it and the honest answer is complicated.

We have taken 12 apprentices over three years. Nine are still with us. Two left for other companies, which is fine and expected. One left the industry.

Cost: an apprentice is roughly 40% of a junior salary, plus the mentoring time, which we measured at about four hours a week for the first six months. Four hours of a senior engineer is not cheap. Total cost per apprentice in year one is close to a junior hire.

Output: by month nine, our apprentices are producing at roughly the level of a junior with a year of experience. By month eighteen there is no distinguishable difference between them and someone we hired conventionally.

So purely financially, it is roughly a wash with a slower ramp.

Why we keep doing it: the nine who stayed have a retention pattern nothing else in our hiring produces. Average tenure is now past three years against a company average of 2.1. And two of them are now the best mentors we have, which I did not anticipate and which I think comes from having been on the other side recently enough to remember it.
